chapter: Micro Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
quiz_title: Micro Ch. 3 Quiz: Supply, Demand, and Equilibrium

questions.stem: Which event causes a **movement along** the demand curve for coffee?

choices.text: A fall in the price of coffee.
choices.why: A change in the good's own price moves buyers along the same demand curve. This is a change in quantity demanded.

choices.text: A rise in consumers' incomes (coffee is a normal good).
choices.why: Income is a non-price determinant. It shifts the whole demand curve to the right rather than moving along it.

choices.text: A change in consumers' tastes toward coffee.
choices.why: Tastes are a non-price determinant. They shift the demand curve.

choices.text: An increase in the number of coffee buyers.
choices.why: The number of buyers is a non-price determinant. It shifts the demand curve.

questions.stem: The price of tea, a substitute for coffee, rises. What happens in the coffee market, holding all else constant?

choices.text: The demand curve for coffee shifts right.
choices.why: Tea became more expensive, so some buyers switch to coffee. Demand for coffee increases at every price.

choices.text: The demand curve for coffee shifts left.
choices.why: That would happen if tea were a complement, or if the price of a substitute fell.

choices.text: There is a movement up along the demand curve for coffee.
choices.why: A movement along the curve requires a change in the price of coffee itself. Here the price of a related good changed.

choices.text: The supply curve for coffee shifts right.
choices.why: The price of tea affects what buyers want, not what coffee sellers offer. Supply does not shift.

questions.stem: Instant noodles are an inferior good. Consumers' incomes rise. What happens to the demand for instant noodles?

choices.why: For an inferior good, higher income lowers demand. Consumers switch to preferred alternatives.
That is the response for a normal good. Inferior goods respond in the opposite direction.

choices.text: Demand does not change, because income is not a determinant of demand.
choices.why: Income is one of the main non-price determinants of demand.

choices.text: There is a movement down along the demand curve.
choices.why: The price of noodles did not change, so there is no movement along the curve. The curve itself shifts.

questions.stem: A frost destroys part of the coffee harvest. Holding demand constant, what happens to the equilibrium price and quantity?

choices.why: The frost shifts supply left. Along an unchanged demand curve, the new intersection has a higher price and a lower quantity.
That describes an increase in supply (a rightward shift), not a decrease.
Both rise only when demand increases. A leftward supply shift cannot raise quantity.
Both fall only when demand decreases. A leftward supply shift raises the price.

questions.stem: Demand is $Q_d = 90 - 3P$ and supply is $Q_s = 10 + 5P$. What is the equilibrium price?

choices.why: This adds the intercepts, $(90+10)/(3+5)$. The intercepts must be subtracted: $a - c$.
This divides by the difference of the slopes, $(90-10)/(5-3)$. The denominator is the sum $b + d$, because both slopes work to push the price toward equilibrium.
This reverses the sign of the numerator, $(10-90)/8$. A negative equilibrium price signals a sign error.

questions.stem: Demand is $Q_d = 120 - 4P$ and supply is $Q_s = 20 + 6P$. What is the equilibrium quantity?

choices.why: $120$ is the quantity demanded at a price of zero (the intercept), not at the equilibrium price.
$20$ is the quantity supplied at a price of zero (the intercept), not at the equilibrium price.
$10$ is the equilibrium price. The question asks for the quantity, which comes from substituting the price into a curve.

questions.stem: In the market $Q_d = 120 - 4P$ and $Q_s = 20 + 6P$, the price is fixed at $P = 8$. What is the situation?

choices.why: At $P=8$, $Q_d = 88$ and $Q_s = 68$. Buyers want more than sellers offer, so there is a shortage of $88 - 68 = 20$.
A surplus requires $Q_s > Q_d$, which happens when the price is above equilibrium ($P > 10$). Here the price is below it.
$88$ is the quantity demanded, not the shortage. The shortage is the gap between $Q_d$ and $Q_s$.
Equilibrium occurs at $P = 10$. At $P = 8$, quantity demanded does not equal quantity supplied.

questions.stem: Demand for coffee increases and, at the same time, supply decreases. What can you say about the new equilibrium?

choices.text: The price rises. The change in quantity is ambiguous.
choices.why: Both shifts push the price up. The demand increase pushes quantity up and the supply decrease pushes it down, so the net effect depends on which shift is larger.

choices.text: The quantity rises. The change in price is ambiguous.
choices.why: The price effect is the unambiguous one here. It is the quantity effect that depends on the relative size of the shifts.
Quantity rises only if the demand shift outweighs the supply shift. It is not guaranteed.

choices.text: The price falls and the quantity is ambiguous.
choices.why: Both a demand increase and a supply decrease raise the price, so the price cannot fall.

questions.stem: Start with $Q_d = 120 - 4P$ and $Q_s = 20 + 6P$. Demand increases to $Q_d = 160 - 4P$. What is the new equilibrium price?

choices.why: $10$ is the original equilibrium price. The demand intercept changed, so the equilibrium price must change too.
$12$ is the equilibrium price when supply falls to $Q_s = 6P$ with the original demand. This question changes demand.
$16$ is the price when demand rises to $160 - 4P$ and supply also falls to $6P$. Only demand changed here.

questions.stem: A news article says: "Because coffee prices rose, demand for coffee fell." Assuming nothing else changed, which statement is the best correction?

choices.text: The rise in price decreased the quantity demanded, a movement along the demand curve. Demand itself did not change.
choices.why: A change in the good's own price moves buyers along the curve. The curve shifts only when a non-price determinant changes.

choices.text: The rise in price shifted the demand curve to the left.
choices.why: This repeats the error. A price change never shifts the demand curve for that same good.

choices.text: The rise in price shifted the supply curve to the left.
choices.why: Supply responds to non-price determinants such as input costs. The price itself is the outcome, not a shifter.

choices.text: The article is correct, because lower quantity demanded always means lower demand.
choices.why: These are different concepts. Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity, while quantity demanded is one point on it.

questions.stem: The FRED series PCOFFOTMUSDM (Global price of Coffee, Other Mild Arabica) is measured in nominal U.S. cents per pound. A student says its rise over ten years proves coffee became more expensive relative to other goods. What is the best response?

choices.text: Not necessarily. The series is nominal, so you must adjust for inflation with a price index to compare real prices.
choices.why: A nominal price can rise simply because the general price level rose. Dividing by a price index such as CPIAUCSL gives a real price.

choices.text: Yes. Any rise in a commodity price means it became more expensive relative to other goods.
choices.why: Relative prices require comparing with other prices. If all prices rose equally, coffee's relative price did not change.

choices.text: No. Commodity prices cannot rise over ten years.
choices.why: Commodity prices can and do rise. The issue is whether the rise reflects inflation or a change in relative price.

choices.text: Yes, because FRED series are already adjusted for inflation.
choices.why: FRED publishes both nominal and real series. The series notes state this one is in nominal U.S. dollars.
